title: AWS Releases Aws-Bench to Evaluate Agents on Cloud Tasks
gist: AWS open-sourced aws-bench, an agent benchmark that scores AI agents against real disposable AWS accounts rather than static fixtures, built on the Harbor framework and supporting Claude Code, Codex, Kiro CLI, Gemini CLI and others; the launch lands amid mounting evidence (a UC Berkeley study) that popular agent benchmarks like Terminal-Bench and SWE-Bench can be gamed to near-perfect scores without solving tasks, and aws-bench itself ships with no baseline results or leaderboard yet.

insights.claim: aws-bench is an open-source benchmark for evaluating how accurately AI agents complete real AWS tasks such as diagnosing misconfigurations, infrastructure provisioning, and operating live cloud environments, using actual resources created in disposable, real AWS accounts rather than static fixtures, which AWS claims gives a more accurate score of agent performance on the work developers and teams actually do.
insights.speaker: Gianmarco Nalin
insights.so_what: Signals AWS's bet that live-environment benchmarking is the credible standard for cloud-agent evaluation, a positioning move that could pull model providers toward optimizing for AWS-specific workflows.
insights.locator: The project claims to take a different approach compared to more traditional static fixtures benchmarks

insights.claim: Each aws-bench scenario deploys AWS resources defined in CDK stacks into an isolated AWS account; once the scenario is live, the agent under evaluation runs its task in a sandboxed container using scoped credentials, and the result is scored by an automated verifier that is either an LLM judge or a programmatic check against live AWS state.
insights.speaker: Gianmarco Nalin
insights.so_what: The reliance on LLM-judge scoring for many tasks is itself a vulnerability flagged later in the article — investors evaluating benchmark credibility should weigh how much of the score depends on programmatic vs. LLM-judge verification.
insights.locator: Each benchmark deploys a scenario in isolated AWS accounts

insights.claim: The benchmark ships with predefined datasets of basic and advanced tasks covering observability, compute and data, databases and storage, EC2 multi-region, serverless, streaming and IoT, reference architectures, and multi-service troubleshooting, and engineering teams can extend the scenarios and tasks to cover their own use cases even though the primary target audience is AI researchers and model providers.
insights.speaker: Gianmarco Nalin
insights.so_what: Broad task coverage across core AWS service categories suggests AWS intends aws-bench to become a general-purpose cloud-agent capability yardstick, not a narrow niche test.
insights.locator: The benchmark comes with predefined datasets

insights.claim: aws-bench is built on Harbor, an open-source framework for evaluating AI agents, extended by AWS to add AWS resource provisioning, scenarios, and verifiers; built-in adapters cover generally available agents and models including Claude Code, Codex, Kiro CLI, and Mini-SWE-Agent, plus any agent already supported by Harbor such as Gemini CLI and OpenCode.
insights.speaker: Gianmarco Nalin
insights.so_what: Multi-agent adapter support (including competitors' agents like Codex and Gemini CLI, not just AWS's own Kiro CLI) signals AWS wants aws-bench to be a neutral, ecosystem-wide standard rather than a vendor-locked showcase for its own tools — worth tracking as a proxy for which coding agents get validated against real cloud infrastructure tasks.
insights.locator: The project is built on Harbor, an open-source framework

insights.claim: Running aws-bench requires more than a local install: credentials with access to the organization's management account and permission to manage member accounts and organizational units, a setup currently pinned to the us-east-1 region, and it creates persistent resources that might incur costs even if unused.
insights.speaker: Gianmarco Nalin
insights.so_what: The high operational and cost barrier to running the benchmark (org-level credentials, real persistent billed resources) limits it mainly to well-resourced model providers/enterprises, not casual users — a practical adoption constraint.
insights.locator: Running the benchmark demands more than a local install

insights.claim: AWS has not published baseline results or a standardized leaderboard for aws-bench at launch, placing both on the future roadmap.
insights.speaker: Gianmarco Nalin
insights.so_what: Absence of baseline scores at launch means there's currently no way to compare agent performance on aws-bench yet — a leaderboard release would be the next catalyst to watch for competitive agent-model positioning on cloud tasks.
insights.locator: Notably absent from the launch are metrics

insights.claim: Researchers from the Center for Responsible, Decentralized Intelligence at UC Berkeley published an article describing how they created an agent that achieved near-perfect scores on some of the most prominent AI agent benchmarks, including Terminal-Bench and SWE-Bench, without solving a single actual task.
insights.speaker: Gianmarco Nalin
insights.so_what: A direct credibility challenge to the two most-cited coding-agent benchmarks in the industry — any model provider's marketing claims based on Terminal-Bench/SWE-Bench scores should now be treated with skepticism pending disclosure of how gaming was achieved.
insights.locator: A group of researchers from the Center for Responsible, Decentralized Intelligence at UC Berkeley

insights.claim: The UC Berkeley researchers state that benchmark gaming is not an isolated incident but a systemic problem: the benchmarks the industry relies on to measure AI capability are themselves vulnerable to the very capabilities they claim to measure.
insights.speaker: Gianmarco Nalin
insights.so_what: Frames benchmark-gaming as a structural, recurring risk rather than a one-off exploit, implying every new agent benchmark (including aws-bench) should be assumed vulnerable until proven resistant to exploitation.
insights.quote: These are not isolated incidents. They are symptoms of a systemic problem: the benchmarks we rely on to measure AI capability are themselves vulnerable to the very capabilities they claim to measure.
insights.locator: In the report, the researchers state

insights.claim: Most aws-bench tasks are evaluated using an LLM judge, and AWS itself documents that leftover state in the disposable AWS accounts can produce unwanted passes or random failures, meaning the benchmark's resistance to exploitation will face scrutiny as adoption grows.
insights.speaker: Gianmarco Nalin
insights.so_what: AWS's own documented weaknesses (LLM-judge reliance, leftover-state scoring noise) mean aws-bench inherits the same integrity risks the UC Berkeley study raised about other benchmarks — a concrete near-term test case for whether the industry can build a gaming-resistant cloud-agent benchmark.
insights.locator: As adoption grows, the benchmark's resistance to exploitation will be under scrutiny
